title: Graphs and Breadth-First Search
tagline: Learn how a computer finds the route with the fewest edges, before the topic comes up in the COS212 lecture.
goal: Arrive at the COS212 graphs lecture able to describe an undirected, unweighted graph and trace breadth-first search on it by hand.
about: Maps, social networks and delivery apps all answer the same kind of question: how are things connected, and what is the quickest way from one to another? Computer scientists answer it with a graph, which is just dots joined by lines.

In this course you work with one small graph, six vertices named A to F, and learn breadth-first search: a method that explores outward one step at a time, like ripples on water. By the end you can trace it by hand and run it in Python.

objectives.text: Describe a graph using the words vertex, edge and neighbour, and spot an isolated vertex.
List the neighbours of any vertex from a picture or a Python adjacency list.
Trace breadth-first search with a queue, showing the queue after every step.
Explain why a vertex is marked as found when it joins the queue.
Find the route with the fewest edges, and identify vertices that can't be reached.
objectives.checked: Route quick check; checks R5 and R6

glossary.meaning: Vertices (dots) joined by edges (lines). It shows how things are connected.
A dot: one thing in the graph, such as A.
A line joining exactly two vertices, such as A–B.
How many edges touch a vertex. C has degree 3.
A vertex with no edges, like F.
Edges have no numbers on them. Every edge counts as one step.
A dictionary from each vertex to the list of its neighbours.
A line: join at the back, served from the front. First in, first out (FIFO).
A pile: the newest item comes off first. Last in, first out (LIFO).
All the vertices the same number of edges from the start.
Marked the moment a vertex joins the queue, so it never joins twice.
Explores outward level by level, using a queue.
The vertex being served when another vertex was found.
The number of edges on a route (not the number of vertices).
No chain of edges leads there from the start.

default_questions: Why is a vertex marked as found when it joins the queue, not when it's served?
What changes if the edges have distances, like kilometres?
How do we search a graph that's in separate pieces?
